lessons.title: Raw Material Characterization
lessons.body: Before you charge any material into a furnace, you must know exactly what you are dealing with. Raw material characterization means testing your ores, fluxes, and fuels to understand their chemical and physical properties. In Africa, common smelting materials include iron ore from Nigeria or South Africa, copper concentrates from Zambia or DRC, and locally sourced limestone and dolomite. Start by taking a representative sampleâabout 5 kg from different parts of your stockpileâand send it to a lab for X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis. This tells you the percentage of iron, silica, alumina, sulfur, and other elements. For a typical iron ore, you want Fe above 60%, silica below 8%, and alumina below 3% for efficient smelting. If your ore has high sulfur (above 0.1%), you may need to roast it first. Physical tests matter too: measure moisture content by drying a 1 kg sample at 105Â°C for 24 hours. High moisture wastes heat and can cause explosions. Also check particle sizeâlumps between 10 mm and 30 mm work best in a blast furnace; fines below 5 mm must be sintered or pelletized. Use a simple sieve set (5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm) to check size distribution. Hardness and porosity affect reduction speed; a drop test from 2 meters onto a steel plate shows if the ore crumbles. Record all results in a logbook. Without characterization, you are guessing, and guessing wastes fuel, flux, and time. A small lab kit with a moisture balance, sieve set, and portable XRF (if affordable) can be set up for under $5,000. Many African smelters fail because they skip this step. Do it right, and your furnace will run smoother.

lessons.title: Weighing and Blending of Charge
lessons.body: Once you know your raw materials, you must weigh and blend them in the correct proportions. The charge is the mixture of ore, flux, and fuel (coke or charcoal) that goes into the furnace. A typical iron blast furnace charge might be 1,600 kg of ore, 400 kg of coke, and 200 kg of limestone per batch. But these numbers depend on your ore analysis. Use a simple formula: for every 100 kg of ore, add flux based on the ratio of silica to lime you need. If your ore has 10% silica, you need about 20 kg of limestone (which is 95% CaCO3) to neutralize it. Weighing must be accurate to within 1%. A platform scale with 0.5 kg resolution is adequate for small operations. For larger ones, use a weigh hopper with load cells. Blending means mixing the materials thoroughly before charging. In Africa, many small foundries use manual mixing on a concrete pad with shovelsâturn the pile three times. But for consistent results, a rotary drum mixer or a cement mixer works better. Mix for at least 5 minutes. The goal is a homogeneous blend so that every scoop has the same ratio. If you skip blending, you get hot spots and cold spots in the furnace, leading to poor metal quality and high fuel consumption. Also, consider preheating or drying the charge if moisture is above 5%. Store blended charge in a covered bin to prevent rain from changing moisture. Keep a batch record: date, ore source, weights, and mixer time. This traceability helps you troubleshoot when something goes wrong. Remember, a good blend is the foundation of a good smelt.

lessons.title: Fluxes and Their Role in Smelting
lessons.body: Fluxes are materials added to the charge to remove impurities and make the slag flow easily. The most common fluxes are limestone (calcium carbonate), dolomite (calcium magnesium carbonate), and silica sand. In African smelting, limestone is often mined locallyâfor example, in Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya. The main job of flux is to combine with unwanted oxides like silica (SiO2) and alumina (Al2O3) to form a slag that melts at a lower temperature than the ore. Without flux, these impurities would thicken the slag, block the furnace, and contaminate the metal. The key concept is basicity: the ratio of basic oxides (CaO, MgO) to acidic oxides (SiO2, Al2O3). For iron smelting, you want a basicity ratio (CaO/SiO2) between 1.0 and 1.2. If your ore is acidic (high silica), add more limestone. If your ore is basic (high lime), add silica sand. You calculate the amount of flux using the formula: Flux (kg) = (Ore kg Ã %SiO2 Ã 1.2) / %CaO in flux. For example, 1,000 kg of ore with 10% SiO2 needs 120 kg of pure CaO. If limestone is 95% CaO, you need 126 kg. Flux also affects slag viscosity. A good slag flows like honey at 1,300â1,400Â°C. If it is too thick, add fluorspar (CaF2) in small amounts (1â2% of charge) but avoid excess as it attacks refractory. Dolomite is useful when you need magnesium oxide to protect the furnace lining. Always test your flux by mixing a small batch and melting it in a crucible to see how it flows. Store fluxes dryâmoisture makes them sticky and hard to weigh. In Africa, many smelters use agricultural limestone, which is cheap but may have high silica; check the analysis. Proper fluxing saves energy and improves metal recovery.

lessons.title: Charging Systems and Equipment
lessons.body: Charging is the process of feeding the prepared charge into the furnace. The equipment you choose depends on furnace type and scale. For small African operations, a manual charging system with a wheelbarrow and a charging chute is common. But for consistent production, you need a mechanical system. The most basic is a skip hoist: a bucket on rails that lifts charge to the furnace top and dumps it into a receiving hopper. A skip hoist can handle 500â2,000 kg per trip and costs around $10,000â$30,000. For larger furnaces, a conveyor belt with a weigh feeder is better. The belt carries charge continuously and can be controlled to match feed rate. In a blast furnace, you also need a double bell or a bell-less top (rotating chute) to distribute charge evenly and seal the furnace gas. A double bell system uses two cones that open alternately to prevent gas escape. A bell-less top uses a rotating chute to place material in specific patternsâthis gives better control of burden distribution. For small cupolas, a simple charging door with a manual chute works. Key equipment includes: a charging hopper (to store blended charge), a weigh hopper (to measure each batch), and a charging car or skip. You also need a stockhouse with bins for ore, coke, and flux, each with a weigh feeder. In Africa, many smelters use second-hand equipment from China or India. Ensure your charging system is reliable and easy to maintain. Motors, gearboxes, and belts must be protected from dust and heat. Install limit switches and emergency stops. A well-designed charging system reduces labor, improves safety, and ensures steady furnace operation. Never overload the furnaceâcharge in small, frequent batches rather than one large dump.

lessons.title: Burden Distribution in Blast Furnace
lessons.body: Burden distribution refers to how the solid charge (ore, coke, flux) is arranged inside the blast furnace. It is critical because it affects gas flow, heat transfer, and chemical reactions. In a blast furnace, the charge descends while hot gases rise. If the burden is not distributed properly, gas will take the path of least resistanceâusually along the wallsâleaving the center cold and inefficient. The ideal distribution has more coke in the center and more ore near the walls. Why? Coke is larger and more permeable, so it allows gas to flow up the center. Ore is finer and less permeable, so it should be near the walls where it can be heated by the descending charge and rising gas. To achieve this, you control the charging pattern. In a bell-less top, you can set the chute to rotate and tilt to different angles. Common patterns are: center coke charging (coke to center, ore to periphery), and mixed charging (alternating layers). For a double bell, you can adjust the stockline (the level of charge) and the size of the bells. A higher stockline gives a flatter profile; a lower one gives a deeper center. You also control the ore-to-coke ratio in each batch. In Africa, many small blast furnaces use manual charging, which makes uniform distribution hard. But you can still improve by charging in small piles around the circumference. Use a template to guide where you dump each skip. Monitor the furnace by checking the temperature of the top gas and the color of the slag. If the center is too cold, add more coke to the center. If the walls are overheating, add more ore near the walls. Burden distribution is a dynamic skillâadjust as conditions change. Proper distribution can cut coke consumption by 10â20% and increase production.

lessons.title: Feed Rate Control and Automation
lessons.body: Feed rate control means regulating how fast charge enters the furnace to match the smelting rate. If you feed too fast, the furnace floods, gas flow is blocked, and you get poor reduction. If you feed too slow, the furnace cools down and production drops. The correct feed rate depends on furnace size, blast volume, and charge composition. For a small blast furnace producing 5 tonnes per day, you might feed 200 kg of charge every 10 minutes. For a larger one (50 tonnes per day), feed 1,000 kg every 5 minutes. The key is to keep the stockline steadyâthe charge level should stay within 0.5 meters of the target. You can measure stockline with a mechanical probe or a radar sensor. Manual control uses a timer and a weigh hopper: the operator opens the hopper gate for a set time, then closes it. But this is inconsistent. Automation uses a programmable logic controller (PLC) to control the feed rate based on signals from the stockline sensor and gas analysis. A simple automated system includes: a weigh feeder on the conveyor, a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the motor, and a PLC that adjusts belt speed to maintain the desired feed rate. For African smelters, cost-effective automation can be built with an Arduino or Raspberry Pi, a load cell, and a motor driver. You can also automate the charging sequence: when the stockline drops, the PLC starts the skip hoist, weighs the charge, and dumps it. Automation reduces labor, improves safety, and gives consistent results. But you must maintain sensors and calibrate weigh scales weekly. Start with manual control, then upgrade step by step. Even a simple timer-based system is better than random feeding. Always keep a log of feed rate, stockline, and furnace conditions to spot trends.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of raw material characterization?
options: A) To determine the color of the ore
B) To know the chemical and physical properties of materials
C) To calculate the furnace temperature
D) To measure the weight of the charge
quiz.explanation: Characterization tests chemical composition and physical properties to guide charging decisions.

quiz.q: Which test measures moisture content in raw materials?
quiz.explanation: Moisture is determined by drying a sample in an oven at 105Â°C until constant weight.

quiz.q: What is the ideal particle size range for lumps in a blast furnace?
quiz.explanation: Lumps between 10 mm and 30 mm provide good permeability and reduction.

quiz.q: Why is blending of charge important?
options: A) To make the charge look uniform
B) To ensure every scoop has the same composition
C) To increase the weight of the charge
D) To reduce the moisture content
quiz.explanation: Homogeneous blending prevents hot spots and ensures consistent smelting.

quiz.q: What is the typical weight of ore in a small blast furnace charge per batch?
quiz.explanation: A typical charge might include 1,600 kg of ore, 400 kg of coke, and 200 kg of limestone.

quiz.q: How many times should you turn a pile when manual mixing?
quiz.explanation: Turning the pile three times helps achieve a homogeneous blend.

quiz.q: What is the main role of flux in smelting?
options: B) To remove impurities and lower slag melting point
quiz.explanation: Flux combines with impurities to form a fluid slag that can be tapped.

quiz.q: What is the desired basicity ratio (CaO/SiO2) for iron smelting?
quiz.explanation: A basicity ratio of 1.0-1.2 gives good slag properties for iron smelting.

quiz.q: Which material is a common flux in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Limestone is widely available and used as a flux in African smelting.

quiz.q: What is the formula to calculate flux needed?
quiz.explanation: This formula calculates the limestone required to neutralize silica in the ore.

quiz.q: What is a skip hoist used for?
options: B) Lifting charge to the furnace top
quiz.explanation: A skip hoist is a mechanical system that lifts and dumps charge into the furnace.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a double bell system in a blast furnace?
options: B) To seal the furnace and prevent gas escape
quiz.explanation: The double bell allows charging while preventing furnace gas from escaping.

quiz.q: Which charging system gives better control of burden distribution?
options: C) Bell-less top with rotating chute
quiz.explanation: A bell-less top with a rotating chute allows precise placement of charge.

quiz.q: What is the ideal burden distribution in a blast furnace?
options: A) More ore in center, more coke at walls
B) More coke in center, more ore at walls
quiz.explanation: Coke in center improves gas permeability, while ore at walls enhances reduction.

quiz.q: Why should there be more coke in the center of the burden?
options: B) To allow gas to flow up the center
quiz.explanation: Coke is more permeable, so gas flows easily through the center.

quiz.q: What is the stockline?
options: A) The level of charge in the furnace
B) The temperature of the top gas
C) The weight of the charge
D) The size of the furnace
quiz.explanation: Stockline is the height of the charge surface inside the furnace.

quiz.q: How can you improve burden distribution in a manually charged furnace?
options: A) Charge in one large pile
B) Charge in small piles around the circumference
quiz.explanation: Charging in small piles around the circumference helps distribute material more evenly.

quiz.q: What is the consequence of feeding charge too fast?
options: B) Furnace floods and gas flow is blocked
quiz.explanation: Too fast feeding can flood the furnace and hinder gas flow.

quiz.q: For a small blast furnace producing 5 tonnes per day, what is a typical feed rate?
quiz.explanation: A 5-tonne-per-day furnace requires about 200 kg of charge every 10 minutes.

quiz.q: What sensor is used to measure stockline?
quiz.explanation: Radar sensors are commonly used to measure the charge level in the furnace.

quiz.q: What does a PLC do in feed rate control?
options: B) Adjusts feed rate based on sensor signals
quiz.explanation: A PLC automates feed rate by controlling motors and feeders based on inputs.

quiz.q: Why is automation beneficial in charging?
options: C) It improves safety and consistency
D) It eliminates the need for weighing
quiz.explanation: Automation reduces manual errors, improves safety, and gives consistent feed.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective automation platform for African smelters?
quiz.explanation: Arduino and Raspberry Pi are affordable and can be used for basic automation.

quiz.q: How often should weigh scales be calibrated?
quiz.explanation: Weekly calibration ensures accurate weighing and consistent charge composition.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of high moisture in the charge?
options: B) Wastes heat and can cause explosions
quiz.explanation: Moisture absorbs heat and can cause steam explosions if suddenly vaporized.

quiz.q: What does XRF analysis measure?
quiz.explanation: XRF (X-ray fluorescence) determines the elemental composition of a sample.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a drop test?
options: B) To check ore hardness and resistance to breakage
quiz.explanation: A drop test assesses how easily ore crumbles under impact.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical flux?
quiz.explanation: Coke is a fuel, not a flux; fluxes are limestone, dolomite, and silica.

quiz.q: What happens if slag is too viscous?
quiz.explanation: High viscosity slag cannot be tapped and may block the furnace.

quiz.q: What is the recommended stockline variation?
quiz.explanation: Keeping stockline within 0.5 meters ensures stable furnace operation.
